::: {.why}
The gap between where you thought the time went and where it went is the reason optimisation without measurement is a hobby rather than an engineering practice.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Profile a real pipeline and identify the actual bottleneck, with numbers.
- State the rule you will follow before any optimisation, and record a baseline you can compare against.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Analyse last night's profile properly: total time, the top functions by cumulative and by self time, and the fraction spent in your code against in libraries. Then run a line profiler on the single worst function. The bottleneck is usually a data conversion or a loop over a dataframe rather than the computation you were worried about.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Establish a baseline harness: a script that runs your three heaviest operations and reports their timings, committed and re-runnable. Every optimisation for the rest of the phase is measured against it, and a change that does not move it does not go in.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Sheppard — Python for Econometrics (notes)](https://bashtage.github.io/kevinsheppard.com/teaching/python/notes/) [textbook]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A profile of your slowest step with the real bottleneck identified, plus a committed benchmark harness with baseline timings.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Where did you think your pipeline's time was going, and where was it actually going?
:::
